Distance from Each Segment Down to the Nearest River

Source: R/frs_near_river.R
frs_near_river.Rd

For every segment of a segmented streams table whose own discharge is below a threshold, walks the network downstream and records the distance to the nearest segment carrying at least that discharge. A habitat rule's near_river condition reads the result, so a small stream close to a large river can pass a rule whose size test it fails (see frs_habitat_predicates()). frs_habitat_classify() calls this itself when a rule asks; call it directly to inspect the distances.

Usage

frs_near_river(conn, table, to, discharge_min, distance_max, verbose = TRUE)

Arguments

conn

A DBI::DBIConnection object (from frs_db_conn()).

table

Character. Schema-qualified segmented streams table with id_segment, watershed_group_code, blue_line_key, watershed_key, downstream_route_measure, wscode_ltree, localcode_ltree, edge_type, waterbody_key, length_metre, mad_m3s and geom.

to

Character. Schema-qualified output table, created if it does not exist, with columns id_segment, watershed_group_code, discharge_min, distance_max and dist_m. A near_river rule reads only rows of its own exact pair, so build the table with the pairs the rules carry (frs_habitat_classify() does): a walk at a longer distance does not serve a rule with a shorter one. Rows for the watershed groups in table are replaced on every call; other groups' rows are kept.

discharge_min

Numeric vector. River discharges to find (m3/s), each finite and above zero.

distance_max

Numeric vector, one per discharge_min. Farthest distance (m) to record for that pair. Each pair is walked on its own, so a pair's distances never depend on the other pairs in the call; pairs must be distinct.

verbose

Logical. Print rows written, segments with no local code, and timing. Default TRUE.

Value

conn invisibly, for pipe chaining.

Details

The walk follows main flow (blue_line_key = watershed_key), as the other downstream traces in fresh do, so a side channel starts on the main stem below it.

Where the distance starts and ends.

  • It starts at the segment's downstream end, so a long segment whose lower end is within the distance passes whole.

  • It ends at the bank of the river, not at its centreline. Where a tributary meets a river drawn as a polygon, its line crosses the polygon as a connector (FWA edge types 1400 and 1450) to the centreline. A connector carries the tributary's own small flow, so it is never a target, and the connector inside the target's polygon (same waterbody_key) is left out of the distance. FWA draws about a third of connectors as side lines, which the walk does not follow; the walk then jumps from the tributary's mouth to the centreline, and that jump is left out too. A connector inside a polygon the walk only passes through, because that river is too small, stays in the distance.

  • Any other jump between consecutive rows of the path is counted at its straight length: a side channel the walk does not follow, or a stretch of river outside table that the path leaves and re-enters.

  • Where a tributary joins its parent follows FWA's local codes, as in every downstream trace in fresh. Where a code places the confluence away from where the lines meet, the distance can differ from a walk that enters at the nearest point, either way: longer by a counted jump, or shorter by the stretch between the two points.

Which segments are measured. Only segments whose own mad_m3s is NULL or below discharge_min get a row: a river large enough to be a target passes or fails on its own size test, never on its distance to itself. A segment with NULL mad_m3s is never a target.

Limits.

  • The walk sees only table. A working table holds one watershed group, so a river beyond the group's outlet is not found.

  • To stay fast, the walk joins only rows within distance_max (plus the longest connector run) in a straight line, and cuts the path where a row it skipped was directly above the next row on that row's line. A path that jumps out of that reach and comes back in a way that test cannot see (the skipped run ends a line, or the row above is out of step with its local code) can read short. It needs a jump between path rows; none occurs on BULK at 3 m3/s within 1 or 20 km.

  • A segment with no local watershed code (localcode_ltree NULL), which is most side channels (edge types 1100, 1150, 1350), has no place in FWA_Downstream()'s ordering. It never walks, so it gets no row and never passes on near_river. Their count is reported when verbose.

See also

Examples

if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{
conn <- frs_db_conn()

# Segments within 1 km of a river carrying 3 m3/s, BULK working table
frs_near_river(conn, "working_bulk.streams", "working_bulk.near_river",
  discharge_min = 3, distance_max = 1000)

DBI::dbGetQuery(conn, "
  SELECT count(*) AS n, round(avg(dist_m)) AS mean_m
  FROM working_bulk.near_river WHERE discharge_min = 3")

DBI::dbDisconnect(conn)
} # }
